approved: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Cash Bidding) Bill 2013
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change how offshore oil and gas exploration permits are allocated in certain areas, using a cash bidding system.
The government says this method would stop unnecessary exploration in regions where little or none is needed, and keep the release of those areas fair and efficient.
A reserve price for each block would be set by the Joint Authority before bids are invited, and could be either made public or kept secret.
Limits the ability to turn down a permit offer to the highest bidder, encouraging real bids.
Creates a separate pre-qualification step to check bidders' technical and financial ability before they place cash bids.
Adds a tie-breaker rule for when two or more cash bids are identical.
Companies that bid for offshore petroleum exploration permits in mature or known resource areas.

Supported the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Cash Bidding) Bill, noting Australia's LNG production is set to grow from under 15 million tonnes 20 years ago to more than 100 million tonnes by 2020, and cited the Montara oil spill as a reminder of the need for strong safety regulation alongside the new cash bidding system for exploration acreage.

Referred the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Cash Bidding) Bill 2013 and the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Regulatory Levies) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

Supported the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment Bill, prompted by the Montara wellhead blow-out on 21 August 2009 in which 69 personnel were safely evacuated but an estimated 29,600 barrels of oil spilled, making it Australia's third largest oil spill after the 1991 Kirki disaster.

Supported the offshore petroleum cash bidding bill, explaining its two-stage process assessing an applicant's suitability before allowing a cash bid for exploration permits, said unsuccessful bidders who withdraw would forfeit a 10 per cent deposit, and welcomed the added transparency and fairness this brings to permit allocation.

Argued that the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Cash Bidding) Bill 2013 gets the balance right between environmental protection and permits, noting bidders must pay in full within 14 days and forfeit a 10 per cent deposit if they refuse an offer.

Argued that the bill borrows competitive bidding elements from the Queensland Mineral Resources Act, having worked in that legislative area previously, and noted that the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax has raised $25 billion to $28 billion in revenue for the Commonwealth government.

Supported the cash bidding bill, citing a budget prediction of around $160 million in additional revenue, and warned that new Gladstone gas export trains will draw so much gas from the east coast that domestic natural gas prices could double by 2020.

Closed debate on the cash bidding bills, explaining that a 10 per cent deposit will discourage frivolous bids and that unsuccessful bidders can appeal under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act, and confirmed the National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator will recover its annual titles administration costs through the new levy.

Moved to schedule non-controversial government bills for consideration from 12:45 pm, including amendments to the Australian Civilian Corps, Import Processing Charges, Grape and Wine Authority, Offshore Petroleum, Rural Research and Development, and Customs Anti-Dumping Commission. Also moved to set general business order for the day, prioritising Senator Moore's motion on pre-election commitments and government document orders.
